children.text: A river that flows about
8km
beneath a limestone mountain before emptying straight into the sea — a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the New7Wonders of Nature. The tour of about
45 minutes
, aboard a small paddled boat into the stalactite cave, is an unmissable Palawan experience.
The Puerto Princesa Underground River is near the village of Sabang, about
80km
northwest of Puerto Princesa city on Palawan's west coast. Flowing about
8.2km

through the limestone beneath Mount Saint Paul, the river runs straight out to the sea from inside the cave, and unusually, its lower reaches are affected by the tides. This has created a unique ecosystem inside the cave where fresh water and seawater mix.
The river and surrounding forest are protected as the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park, and were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in
. In

it was also chosen as one of the "New7Wonders of Nature," cementing its place as one of the Philippines' signature attractions. The park holds an intact ecosystem stretching from the mountaintop down to the sea, home to a variety of animals such as long-tailed macaques, monitor lizards, hornbills, and bats.
Visitors take a bangka from Sabang pier to the beach at the cave entrance, then switch to a small boat rowed by a guide for a round trip of about

inside the cave. As you go in wearing a helmet and listening to an audio guide, the beam of a flashlight reveals stalactites and stalagmites formed over millions of years. Guides playfully name the rock formations things like the Holy Family, the cathedral, and a fruit-and-vegetable market. Bats and swiftlets live in colonies on the cave ceiling.
The park's history begins with Proclamation No. 835 on
March 26, 1971
, which designated the St. Paul Subterranean National Park (about 3,901 hectares). Proclamation No. 212 on
November 16, 1999
expanded the area to 22,202 hectares and gave the park its present name, and on
December 4
of the same year it was inscribed as a natural World Heritage site. The New7Wonders of Nature title was provisionally announced on
November 11, 2011
and officially confirmed on
January 28, 2012
. The limestone enclosing the cave formed about 16–20 million years ago, and Mount Saint Paul,
high, rises above it. Of the river's total
8.2km
, the section that can be entered by boat is
4.3km
according to the official website; the largest space in the cave, the Italian Chamber, is about
long, and the ceiling of the cathedral chamber reaches a height of about
. More than 165 bird species have been recorded in the park, and all 15 Palawan endemic species can be seen there.

Daily entry is limited and requires a permit, which takes a bit of preparation, but it's an easy day trip from Puerto Princesa. It's recommended for families, travelers wanting nature-documentary-style scenery, and anyone visiting Palawan for the first time.
A guide rows you through the cave for about
45 minutes
. The person at the bow often gets to shine the flashlight, so sitting up front gives a more vivid experience.
A wide chamber with a high ceiling, where the stalactites resemble a cathedral's pillars and altar. It's considered the highlight of the cave tour.
A community-run tour on a small boat through the mangrove waterways near Sabang village. You can see snakes and birds up in the trees and the mangrove ecosystem up close.

blocks.title: Wildlife watching at the cave-entrance beach

children.text: While waiting your turn for a boat, you can easily spot long-tailed macaques and large monitor lizards in the forest by the beach. Don't feed them or approach too closely.
After the tour, you can swim at Sabang Beach or enjoy lunch at a beach resort. A quiet beach backed by limestone mountains.
A limestone rock formation on the way from Puerto Princesa to Sabang, offering a short climb through the cave and a zipline at the top.
A zipline crossing the sea sometimes operates near Sabang Beach. Check on-site whether it's currently running.
A trail of about
5.3km
that crosses the forest from Sabang to the cave entrance. The official website says it is open
8 AM–3 PM

, but at the time of checking it was temporarily closed for maintenance work. If it is open, you can see the forest and wildlife on foot instead of by boat, so confirm whether it is open before you set out.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night (overnight in Sabang)
items.subtitle: Itinerary aiming for the first boat of the morning

children.text: At the booking office in Puerto Princesa city, check the date and name on your permit for the next day.
Take a van from the Irawan terminal to Sabang, about
2–2.5 hours
away, and settle in at your Sabang lodging.
Watch the sunset at Sabang Beach, which faces the western sea, and have grilled fish for dinner at a beach restaurant.
At the Sabang pier registration desk, hand in your permit, pay the fees, and receive a boat number ticket. Lining up early means a shorter wait.
Take a bangka to the cave-entrance beach, about
15–20 minutes
Take the underground river boat tour. It takes about
45 minutes
, and you wear a life jacket and helmet.
Ride the Sabang river mangrove paddle boat, or swim at the beach.
Have lunch, then take a van back to the city in the afternoon. Check the last departure time the day before.

items.title: Independent travel (DIY) day trip
items.subtitle: Going on your own by van

children.text: Secure your permit at the booking office. The office is open
7:30 AM–5 PM
Arrive at the Irawan terminal and board a van or the first bus to Sabang.
Arrive at Sabang pier, pay the entrance fee, environmental fee, audio guide, and bangka fare in cash, and receive a helmet, life jacket, and audio device.
Wait for your number to be called. On busy days the wait reaches
2–3 hours
. You can ride the mangrove paddle boat while you wait.
Head to the cave-entrance beach, finish the underground river tour, and return to Sabang.
Have lunch, check the last departure time, and head back to the city.
Waits can be long, so the earlier you get your number ticket, the easier your day will be. Even with the same permit, your boat turn depends on the order in which you arrive.
Many direct flights connect Manila, Cebu, and Clark to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS). From Manila it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
, at around
one way — the cheapest way in among Palawan's airports. The airport is in the city center, about
10 minutes
by tricycle.

The Manila–Puerto Princesa route is operated by Cebu Pacific, Philippine Airlines, and AirAsia Philippines, with several flights a day. From Cebu, Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines fly direct in about
1 hour 15 minutes
, and from Clark a direct Cebu Pacific flight takes about
1 hour 25 minutes
. Clark flights are less frequent, so check the operating days before you plan your schedule. The airport is about
2km
from the city center; a tricycle costs about
and a shared airport van about
The easiest way is a day tour of the underground river from a travel agency in the city. It includes round-trip hotel pickup, the permit, the entrance fee, the boat, and lunch, at about
per person. To go on your own, take a van or jeepney to Sabang from the Irawan terminal, about 30 minutes from the city; it takes about
2–2.5 hours
and costs about
. Chartering a vehicle costs about
per vehicle.
The Irawan terminal is the city's integrated transport terminal, relocated from San Jose in
January 2023
, about
12km
from the city center. From Rizal Avenue in the city or in front of the airport, take a multicab marked "Irawan Terminal" for about
30 minutes
and about
. The first vehicles to Sabang leave early in the morning, so to make it in time for a morning tour slot, it is best to reach the terminal by
7 AM
at the latest.
From the Sabang pier to the cave entrance beach, only bangkas licensed by the national park operate, taking about
15–20 minutes
. The bangka fare is
per person (minimum 6 people,
per boat), and you gather a group and share the boat. If the waves are high, bangka service stops and the tour is canceled.

The Underground River limits daily entry to 900 people, and the official website states that it strictly enforces a "NO PERMIT, NO ENTRY" rule. Before your visit you must obtain an entry permit at the Underground River booking office in Puerto Princesa city, and staying in Sabang does not guarantee a permit. Many notices say permit processing takes several days, and applying in person on the day mostly fails, so booking through a travel agency is the surest option in peak season, and you should apply as early as possible once your dates are set.
The booking office is in Mendoza Park in Barangay Model in Puerto Princesa city, about
10 minutes
by car from the airport. When applying, you must show ID and be registered one person at a time. The cave tour operates only
8 AM–4 PM
, avoiding the times when bats and swiftlets come and go. Announcements can be checked on the
official Underground River National Park website
Independent visitors submit their ID and visitor list at the booking office to confirm a date. The office is open daily
7:30 AM–5 PM
, and the Sabang pier office opens
8 AM–5 PM

. Once you have a permit, you pay the fees at the Sabang pier registration desk on the day of your visit and receive a boat number ticket. The park's operating hours are written differently on two pages of the official website,
8 AM–4 PM
and
, so it is best to avoid plans that arrive late in the day.
Driving about
80km
north from Puerto Princesa city along the national highway brings you to Sabang. Mountain roads and coastal roads alternate, so it takes about
2–2.5 hours
. Chartering a van from the city costs about
, varying greatly by operator and what is included. If you drive yourself, there are no ATMs in Sabang, so fill up on fuel in the city and bring cash.
Ugong Rock (about
1 hour
from the city) lies along the way, so stopping there on the way to and from Sabang in a chartered vehicle is a popular itinerary.

items.title: Getting to El Nido and Port Barton

children.text: From Puerto Princesa to El Nido is about
260km
. A Cherry Bus ordinary seat costs about
, a comfortable seat about
, and a shared van about
, taking
5–6 hours
. To Port Barton, a van takes about
3 hours 30 minutes
and costs about
. There are few or no regular services from Sabang straight to Port Barton or El Nido, or the times change often, so it is usual to return to the city and transfer, or to use a chartered vehicle.
November
through
May
is the dry season and good for visiting.
January
through
April
especially has little rain and a calm sea, so bangka service runs reliably. During Holy Week and summer break (
March–May
), Filipino family travelers crowd in, making permits hard to get, so book early.
From
June
to
October

is the rainy season under the southwest monsoon Habagat, and the west coast where Sabang sits gets rougher seas, causing days when bangka service is suspended. Heavy rain can also swell the river and suspend the cave tour. It's best to build in a buffer day for this period, and confirm on the morning of your trip whether the tour operator is running. The park sometimes closes temporarily for maintenance or bad weather, so check the latest notices.
Inside the cave it's cooler than outside but humid, and the beach at the cave entrance has strong sun, so prepare for both environments.
The park closed on

for maintenance and ecological recovery, and it is reported that in some years it closes at the same time. If you are traveling in early July, be sure to check the park's latest notices. Competition for permits is fiercest during the late December to early January holidays, Holy Week (late March in 2027), and the April–May school break.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Most people stay in Puerto Princesa city and visit as a day trip. The city has many guesthouses and mid-range hotels at about
per night, and resort-style hotels near the coastal road and airport run about
per night. If you'd rather stay somewhere quiet and natural, an overnight at Sabang Beach is also good. Sabang has bungalow-style lodging and beach resorts (about
per night), letting you catch the first tour early the next morning.

Puerto Princesa is Palawan's culinary city. There are many restaurants serving seafood in various styles, and some, like the long-popular seafood restaurant KaLui, require reservations. Tamilok, a mangrove-dwelling shipworm, is a Palawan specialty eaten raw like oysters, served with a vinegar dip. Palawan cashews and dried fish make good souvenirs. Sabang beach restaurants serve grilled fish and seafood stir-fry for about
per person.
Sabang is a small village with a single road running along the beach, and guesthouses and small resorts start from about
per night. For upscale lodging, Sheridan Beach Resort & Spa on Sabang Beach starts at about
per room, and Daluyon Beach and Mountain Resort from about
US$80
per night. There are no ATMs in Sabang and mobile signal is weak, so check in advance how you can pay for your lodging. Most places to eat are small restaurants and cafés along the beach road.
Permits are limited in number and can sell out weeks ahead in peak season. Book as soon as your dates are set.
There are no ATMs in Sabang, so bring cash from the city. The bangka, entrance fees, and meals are all paid in cash.
Bat droppings can fall inside the cave, so it's best not to look up with your mouth open. Guides give the same warning.
Flash photography is restricted inside the cave. It's a good idea to set your camera up for low light beforehand.
Since a pre-dawn pickup is typical on tour day, it's best to turn in early the night before.
The road to Sabang has many winding mountain sections, so bring motion-sickness medicine if needed.
A dry bag and a light raincoat help protect against spray during the boat ride and sudden showers.
Phone signal in Sabang tends to be weak.
Since
February 2026

, the Sabang pier has been trialing a new boarding registration procedure, so the waiting and registration method may change. It is best to follow on-site instructions and check the official website's announcements in advance.
The on-site payment for an independent visit is the entrance fee
, environmental fee
, audio guide
, and terminal fee
, totaling
; adding the bangka at
per person brings it to about
. Having plenty of small change makes registration faster.
The monkeys and monitor lizards at the cave-entrance beach can be drawn to food bags. Don't take out food, and keep your bag closed and close to your body.
Standing up in the boat or reaching out to touch the stalactites is prohibited inside the cave.
Smoking, eating, and littering are banned inside the national park.
Bangka service is suspended on high-wave days, and if a tour is cancelled, confirm the refund terms with your travel agency in advance.
Park entry rules, fees, and closure days can change by park authority decision, so check the latest notices.
Don't trust touts who claim they can get you a permit on the spot. The official website also warns that staying in Sabang does not guarantee entry.
Monkeys mistake plastic bags for food bags and may also snatch sunglasses. On the beach, keep your bag closed and don't leave sunglasses or plastic bags in view.
An island-hopping destination about
30–40 minutes
from the city by car, good for snorkeling and resting on sandy islets.
A quiet beach town about
3–4 hours
from Sabang via the Roxas-direction road.
Palawan's premier resort town, about
5–6 hours
from Puerto Princesa by van.
About
30 minutes
from the city by car, where you can watch fireflies along a mangrove river at night.
A limestone rock in the village of Tagabinet on the road from Puerto Princesa to Sabang, about
1 hour–1 hour 20 minutes
from the city by car. You can enjoy a short trek up to the summit and a zipline.
